documents.title: Macroeconomic and satellite model reference data set documentation (MSD-RDS v5.0)

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set MSD-RDS v5.0 used to estimate the scenario generation model and the PD and LGD satellite models of the Macroeconomic Scenario and Satellite Models (inventory identifier MDL-10, model version 5.0). The RDS consists of two parts: the macroeconomic data set of 34 quarterly series for the Netherlands, the euro area and financial markets, and the satellite panel of quarterly default rates for 29 credit portfolio segments and annual workout LGD cohorts of the Bank. The model outputs are used for IFRS 9 forward-looking information, for the ICAAP normative and economic perspectives, for the annual Group stress test and reverse stress test and for the credit risk appetite calibration. The scope covers the Bank N.V., its consumer credit subsidiary and its Belgian branch; the Belgian branch's exposures are projected with the Dutch satellite models because its portfolio (EUR 3.1 billion) is too small for separate estimation, as justified in section 5.2. The document follows the RDS documentation template of Annex A of MRM-STD-021 v3.0 and is version-controlled in the controlled document repository under DOC-MDL10-RDS.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The macroeconomic data set covers 122 quarters from 1996Q1 to 2026Q2 for the scenario generation model. The satellite panel covers 94 quarters from 2003Q1 to 2026Q2 for 29 segments (residential mortgages 8, consumer lending 4, retail SME 6, corporates 11), giving 2,726 segment-quarter observations, and is built from 118.6 million obligor-quarter records of 4.9 million unique obligors with 612,400 obligor-level default events. The LGD cohort data contain 41,870 closed workouts of retail SME and corporate obligors with default dates from 2003 to 2022, grouped into 20 annual cohorts. The observation window ends in 2026Q2 because the default outcomes and macroeconomic releases for that quarter were final at the RDS freeze on 16 October 2026. All counts in this document are produced by the build code tagged v5.0.0 from the frozen RDS version MSD-RDS-v5.0-20261016.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The macroeconomic window starts in 1996Q1, the first quarter of consistent CBS quarterly national accounts and ILO unemployment for the Netherlands under ESA 2010, and provides four recessions (2003, 2009, 2012–2013 and 2020) for the estimation of the joint dynamics. The satellite panel starts in 2003Q1, when the Bank's credit risk data warehouse began to store obligor-level arrears and defaults for all portfolios. The panel covers a full economic cycle including the 2008–2013 downturn, with the Dutch house price correction of about 20% from peak to trough and the rise in unemployment to above 7%, as well as the 2020 COVID-19 shock and the 2022–2023 interest rate increase. Data from 2003 onwards thus include the good and bad years relevant for the relationship between macroeconomic variables and default rates, and their representativeness is analysed in chapter 5. For the corporate real estate and construction segments, whose own default history before 2008 is thin, the CBS bankruptcy rate of the corresponding sectors is used as proxy for 2003–2007, and its representativeness is justified in section 5.2.

sections.heading: Target variables and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target variable of the PD satellite models is the quarterly segment default rate, defined as the number of obligors defaulting within four quarters after the reference date divided by the number of performing obligors at the reference date, transformed to logits. The target of the LGD satellite model is the exposure-weighted average realised LGD of each annual default cohort of retail SME and corporate obligors, with recoveries and directly attributable costs discounted at the original effective interest rate. The targets of the scenario generation model are the quarterly macroeconomic series themselves, in growth rates or levels as listed in Annex A. The default events are those of the Bank's definition of default (CR-STD-110), which is also the definition used for IFRS 9 Stage 3, so that the satellite projections are consistent across IFRS 9, stress testing and ICAAP.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: For quarters from 2016Q1 onwards the default flag is taken from the production default register without deviation. For 2003Q1 to 2015Q4 the default flag is approximated from arrears of more than 90 days on an amount above EUR 250 and from restructuring with debt reduction, as described in section 3.3. The approximation does not capture the unlikeliness-to-pay triggers other than restructuring; on the overlap year 2016 it identifies 96.9% of register defaults, and the approximated default rate is 3.1% lower in relative terms, mainly in corporate segments. Because the satellite models explain the variation of default rates over time rather than their level, the level difference is absorbed by the segment fixed effects; a dummy for the approximation period is tested in the MDD and is not significant.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: The default flag follows CR-STD-110: an obligor is in default when a material credit obligation is more than 90 days past due or the obligor is unlikely to pay, with the materiality threshold of EUR 100 and 1% for retail and EUR 500 and 1% for non-retail exposures. The absolute component is compared with the sum of the obligor's past due amounts and the relative component is that sum divided by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure, and days past due are counted from the first day on which both components are exceeded and restart when either is no longer exceeded. The relative component is the 1% set by the ECB, and the regulatory threshold is applied from 31 December 2020, which the flag DOD_MAT_REGIME identifies in the segment-level data. Default is identified at obligor level for all exposure classes, and the date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met. Obligors return to non-default status after a probation period of at least three months, or twelve months after a distressed restructuring, and a re-default within twelve months of return is merged with the earlier default; 29,850 such events were merged in the panel. Probation periods could not be reconstructed for 2003–2015, where cure is assumed on the date the arrears criterion ceased.

sections.heading: Past-due counting in the default register
sections.text: Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on its due date is recognised as past due, and where the payment schedule has been modified, days past due are counted on the modified schedule after an assessment of distressed restructuring. Instalments suspended under the general payment moratoria of 2020, which met the conditions of EBA/GL/2020/02, were not counted as past due; this is the reason for exclusion E4 of the consumer and SME moratoria quarters. The relative component divides the past due amount by the total on-balance-sheet exposure of the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, excluding equity exposures. Days past due are counted daily in the Arrears Management System and the Corporate Loan System, and where a criterion is detected by a less frequent process, the default date is set to the day on which the criterion was actually met. Once the past-due criterion is met the obligor is defaulted without further expert judgement, and all its exposures are flagged as defaulted in every system of the Bank, its subsidiary and its branch within one business day, before the monthly CRDW snapshot is taken. Technical past due is recognised only in the cases listed in EBA/GL/2016/07, such as system errors and payment allocation lags, and each case is documented and corrected within 30 days.

sections.heading: Probation and forbearance
sections.text: A defaulted obligor returns to non-default status only after at least three months without any default trigger and an assessment by Credit Risk Management that the improvement of its financial situation is factual and permanent. After a distressed restructuring, the probation period is at least one year from the latest of the restructuring, the default classification and the end of any grace period, and return requires a material payment, regular payments under the new schedule and no amounts past due or other doubts about full repayment. The probation start date and status are stored for every default event in the default register and are used to identify the merged multiple defaults in the panel. For forbearance measures the diminished financial obligation is computed as the relative reduction in net present value discounted at the original effective interest rate, with a threshold of 1%; forborne exposures below the threshold are assessed for other unlikeliness-to-pay indications, and all forborne non-performing exposures are defaulted, which Credit Risk Management verifies quarterly.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: The unlikeliness-to-pay triggers used in the default register are those of CR-STD-110 §6: non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments and Stage 3 classification, sale of credit obligations at a credit-related loss above 5%, distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%, bankruptcy and forced sale of collateral lead to default automatically. Additional indicators such as fraud, covenant breaches and significant income decline lead to a case-by-case assessment within 30 days. The triggers are mapped to source-system fields in the default engine, whose mapping table is maintained by Credit Risk Management and is not repeated here; the RDS uses only the resulting obligor-level default flag and date. The same definition of default applies to all portfolios of the Bank, its subsidiary and its branch, so that the segment default rates are comparable across portfolios.

sections.heading: Default flag reconciliation
sections.text: The default flag in the satellite panel is constructed in accordance with CR-STD-110, including the materiality thresholds, the UTP triggers, the probation periods and the merging of multiple defaults, for the period in which the default register exists. The segment default counts for 2016Q1–2026Q2 were reconciled with the default counts of the production default register: the counts agree for 99.97% of segment-quarters, and the eight differences stem from retroactive default date corrections after the register extraction. The default rates were also compared with the default rates reported in the IRB and IFRS 9 monitoring reports of the PD models MDL-01, MDL-06 and MDL-07, with differences below 0.01 percentage points for every portfolio and year.

sections.heading: Operationalisation of unlikeliness to pay
sections.text: Non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments resulting from a significant decline in credit quality and all Stage 3 classifications are treated as indications of unlikeliness to pay and lead to default, while Stage 1 and Stage 2 allowances do not. Additional indicators are specified per exposure type for all business lines, legal entities and locations in CR-STD-110, each leading either to automatic default or to a case-by-case assessment. For each indicator, the default engine mapping table utp_map_v7.csv defines the source-system fields, the identification method, the internal and external information sources (BKR credit register, Central Insolvency Register, press and analyst monitoring) and the monitoring frequency, and the outcome of each case-by-case assessment is recorded with its rationale. Manual identification processes such as the watchlist review and insolvency alerts are updated at least weekly, which ensures timely identification of default for the quarterly default rates.

sections.heading: Macroeconomic data sources
sections.text: Macroeconomic series are sourced from CBS Statistics Netherlands (real GDP, unemployment rate, household disposable income, the house price index of existing owner-occupied dwellings), De Nederlandsche Bank (projections), the ECB data portal (3-month Euribor, euro area GDP and HICP, EUR/USD reference rate), the Dutch State Treasury Agency (10-year Dutch government bond yield), MSCI (Netherlands commercial real estate capital value index), S&P Global (iBoxx EUR non-financials spread) and STOXX (EURO STOXX 50). The lineage of these external series starts at the point of receipt in the Bank's market data platform MDP and records the provider, the data product and series code and the delivery date of each vintage; the vintage used for MSD-RDS v5.0 is that of 9 October 2026. The MSCI CRE index is available annually before 2012 and is interpolated to quarterly frequency with the Chow–Lin method using the CBS commercial property transaction price index as indicator; the interpolation is documented as expert judgement EJ-10-01, approved by the model owner on 30 October 2026 and cross-referenced to data deficiency DD-10-02. External data were assessed for fitness for use by comparing each series with an independent second source where available (for example CBS and Eurostat GDP), with differences below 0.05 percentage points.

sections.heading: Internal data sources and lineage

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per series in Annex C: the macroeconomic data set has no missing values after the CRE interpolation, and missing segment default counts (none) would not be imputed. The CRE index interpolation before 2012 affects 64 quarters; the effect of using the alternative Denton method on the corporate real estate satellite coefficient is below 5% of its value. Outliers are identified by the rule of a quarterly change larger than five standard deviations, applied identically in development and in the quarterly production update; the rule flags 2020Q2 GDP (−8.5% quarter on quarter) and the 2020Q2–Q3 unemployment movements, which are retained as genuine observations and handled in the VAR by a COVID-19 dummy for 2020Q2–2020Q4. The dummy reduces the influence of the COVID-19 quarters on the estimated persistence; without it, the half-life of an unemployment shock falls from 7 to 4 quarters.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness was assessed for the macroeconomic data by comparing the historical range of each series with the scenario paths, and for the satellite panel by comparing segment composition and default-rate levels with the current portfolio. The current portfolio composition by segment (share of performing obligors) differs from the 2003–2026 average by less than 3 percentage points for every segment, with a PSI of the segment distribution of 0.04 between the panel average and 2026Q2. The 2025 default rates lie within the historical range of every segment: mortgages 0.29% (range 0.14% to 0.86%), consumer lending 1.81% (1.21% to 3.64%), retail SME 1.58% (0.97% to 3.92%) and corporates 0.41% (0.22% to 2.31%). The ICAAP adverse scenario moves house prices and CRE prices outside the historical range of annual changes; this is addressed by the extrapolation tests described in the MDD, not by the data.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment

Accuracy was confirmed by reconciling the performing obligor counts and exposure per segment to CRDW and, for 2016 onwards, to the exposure reported in FINREP, with differences below 0.1%, and by sample checks of 150 workout LGD records against the workout files, of which 148 were confirmed and two corrected at source. Consistency was assessed over the observation period, including the change in the default definition in 2021, between the RDS and the quarterly production update data, and through logical rules such as defaults not exceeding performing obligors. Timeliness: macroeconomic data are available 45 days after quarter end (CBS flash estimate) and final default counts 20 business days after quarter end.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set MSD-RDS v5.0 used to estimate the scenario generation model and the PD and LGD satellite models of the Macroeconomic Scenario and Satellite Models (inventory identifier MDL-10, model version 5.0). The RDS consists of two parts: the macroeconomic data set of 34 quarterly series for the Netherlands, the euro area and financial markets, and the satellite panel of quarterly default rates for 29 credit portfolio segments and annual workout LGD cohorts of the Bank. The model outputs are used for IFRS 9 forward-looking information, for the ICAAP normative and economic perspectives, for the annual Group stress test and reverse stress test and for the credit risk appetite calibration. The scope covers the Bank N.V., its consumer credit subsidiary and its Belgian branch; the Belgian branch's exposures are projected with the Dutch satellite models because its portfolio (EUR 3.1 billion) is too small for separate estimation, as justified in section 5.2. sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The macroeconomic data set covers 122 quarters from 1996Q1 to 2026Q2 for the scenario generation model. The satellite panel covers 94 quarters from 2003Q1 to 2026Q2 for 29 segments (residential mortgages 8, consumer lending 4, retail SME 6, corporates 11), giving 2,726 segment-quarter observations, and is built from 118.6 million obligor-quarter records of 4.9 million unique obligors with 612,400 obligor-level default events. The LGD cohort data contain 41,870 closed workouts of retail SME and corporate obligors with default dates from 2003 to 2022, grouped into 20 annual cohorts. The observation window ends in 2026Q2 because the default outcomes and macroeconomic releases for that quarter were final at the RDS freeze on 16 October 2026. All counts in this document are produced by the build code tagged v5.0.0 from the frozen RDS version MSD-RDS-v5.0-20261016.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The macroeconomic window starts in 1996Q1, the first quarter of consistent CBS quarterly national accounts and ILO unemployment for the Netherlands under ESA 2010, and provides four recessions (2003, 2009, 2012–2013 and 2020) for the estimation of the joint dynamics. The satellite panel starts in 2003Q1, when the Bank's credit risk data warehouse began to store obligor-level arrears and defaults for all portfolios. The panel covers a full economic cycle including the 2008–2013 downturn, with the Dutch house price correction of about 20% from peak to trough and the rise in unemployment to above 7%, as well as the 2020 COVID-19 shock and the 2022–2023 interest rate increase. Data from 2003 onwards thus include the good and bad years relevant for the relationship between macroeconomic variables and default rates, and their representativeness is analysed in chapter 5. For the corporate real estate and construction segments, whose own default history before 2008 is thin, the CBS bankruptcy rate of the corresponding sectors is used as proxy for 2003–2007, and its representativeness is justified in section 5.2.

sections.heading: Target variables and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target variable of the PD satellite models is the quarterly segment default rate, defined as the number of obligors defaulting within four quarters after the reference date divided by the number of performing obligors at the reference date, transformed to logits. The target of the LGD satellite model is the exposure-weighted average realised LGD of each annual default cohort of retail SME and corporate obligors, with recoveries and directly attributable costs discounted at the original effective interest rate. The targets of the scenario generation model are the quarterly macroeconomic series themselves, in growth rates or levels as listed in Annex A. sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: The default flag follows CR-STD-110: an obligor is in default when a material credit obligation is more than 90 days past due or the obligor is unlikely to pay, with the materiality threshold of EUR 100 and 1% for retail and EUR 500 and 1% for non-retail exposures. The absolute component is compared with the sum of the obligor's past due amounts and the relative component is that sum divided by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure, and days past due are counted from the first day on which both components are exceeded and restart when either is no longer exceeded. The relative component is the 1% set by the ECB, and the regulatory threshold is applied from 31 December 2020, which the flag DOD_MAT_REGIME identifies in the segment-level data. Default is identified at obligor level for all exposure classes, and the date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met. Obligors return to non-default status after a probation period of at least three months, or twelve months after a distressed restructuring, and a re-default within twelve months of return is merged with the earlier default; 29,850 such events were merged in the panel. Probation periods could not be reconstructed for 2003–2015, where cure is assumed on the date the arrears criterion ceased.

sections.heading: Past-due counting in the default register
sections.text: Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on its due date is recognised as past due, and where the payment schedule has been modified, days past due are counted on the modified schedule after an assessment of distressed restructuring. Instalments suspended under the general payment moratoria of 2020, which met the conditions of EBA/GL/2020/02, were not counted as past due; this is the reason for exclusion E4 of the consumer and SME moratoria quarters. The relative component divides the past due amount by the total on-balance-sheet exposure of the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, excluding equity exposures. Days past due are counted daily in the Arrears Management System and the Corporate Loan System, and where a criterion is detected by a less frequent process, the default date is set to the day on which the criterion was actually met. Once the past-due criterion is met the obligor is defaulted without further expert judgement, and all its exposures are flagged as defaulted in every system of the Bank, its subsidiary and its branch within one business day, before the monthly CRDW snapshot is taken. Technical past due is recognised only in the cases listed in EBA/GL/2016/07, such as system errors and payment allocation lags, and each case is documented and corrected within 30 days.

sections.heading: Probation and forbearance
sections.text: A defaulted obligor returns to non-default status only after at least three months without any default trigger and an assessment by Credit Risk Management that the improvement of its financial situation is factual and permanent. After a distressed restructuring, the probation period is at least one year from the latest of the restructuring, the default classification and the end of any grace period, and return requires a material payment, regular payments under the new schedule and no amounts past due or other doubts about full repayment. The probation start date and status are stored for every default event in the default register and are used to identify the merged multiple defaults in the panel. For forbearance measures the diminished financial obligation is computed as the relative reduction in net present value discounted at the original effective interest rate, with a threshold of 1%; forborne exposures below the threshold are assessed for other unlikeliness-to-pay indications, and all forborne non-performing exposures are defaulted, which Credit Risk Management verifies quarterly.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: The unlikeliness-to-pay triggers used in the default register are those of CR-STD-110 §6: non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments and Stage 3 classification, sale of credit obligations at a credit-related loss above 5%, distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%, bankruptcy and forced sale of collateral lead to default automatically. Additional indicators such as fraud, covenant breaches and significant income decline lead to a case-by-case assessment within 30 days. The triggers are mapped to source-system fields in the default engine, whose mapping table is maintained by Credit Risk Management and is not repeated here; the RDS uses only the resulting obligor-level default flag and date. The same definition of default applies to all portfolios of the Bank, its subsidiary and its branch, so that the segment default rates are comparable across portfolios.

sections.heading: Operationalisation of unlikeliness to pay
sections.text: Non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments resulting from a significant decline in credit quality and all Stage 3 classifications are treated as indications of unlikeliness to pay and lead to default, while Stage 1 and Stage 2 allowances do not. Additional indicators are specified per exposure type for all business lines, legal entities and locations in CR-STD-110, each leading either to automatic default or to a case-by-case assessment. For each indicator, the default engine mapping table utp_map_v7.csv defines the source-system fields, the identification method, the internal and external information sources (BKR credit register, Central Insolvency Register, press and analyst monitoring) and the monitoring frequency, and the outcome of each case-by-case assessment is recorded with its rationale. Manual identification processes such as the watchlist review and insolvency alerts are updated at least weekly, which ensures timely identification of default for the quarterly default rates.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per series in Annex C: the macroeconomic data set has no missing values after the CRE interpolation, and missing segment default counts (none) would not be imputed. The CRE index interpolation before 2012 affects 64 quarters; the effect of using the alternative Denton method on the corporate real estate satellite coefficient is below 5% of its value. Outliers are identified by the rule of a quarterly change larger than five standard deviations, applied identically in development and in the quarterly production update; the rule flags 2020Q2 GDP (−8.5% quarter on quarter) and the 2020Q2–Q3 unemployment movements, which are retained as genuine observations and handled in the VAR by a COVID-19 dummy for 2020Q2–2020Q4. The dummy reduces the influence of the COVID-19 quarters on the estimated persistence; without it, the half-life of an unemployment shock falls from 7 to 4 quarters.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness was assessed for the macroeconomic data by comparing the historical range of each series with the scenario paths, and for the satellite panel by comparing segment composition and default-rate levels with the current portfolio. The current portfolio composition by segment (share of performing obligors) differs from the 2003–2026 average by less than 3 percentage points for every segment, with a PSI of the segment distribution of 0.04 between the panel average and 2026Q2. The 2025 default rates lie within the historical range of every segment: mortgages 0.29% (range 0.14% to 0.86%), consumer lending 1.81% (1.21% to 3.64%), retail SME 1.58% (0.97% to 3.92%) and corporates 0.41% (0.22% to 2.31%). The ICAAP adverse scenario moves house prices and CRE prices outside the historical range of annual changes; this is addressed by the extrapolation tests described in the MDD, not by the data.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The effect of each exclusion on segment default rates and on the satellite coefficients was quantified. Exclusion E4 (moratoria quarters) has the largest effect: including these quarters reduces the consumer unemployment coefficient by 11%, because arrears were suppressed while unemployment rose, which confirms that their exclusion avoids a downward bias. Exclusion E1 changes the corporate GDP coefficient by less than 2%; E2 and E3 have no measurable effect. The data therefore remain relevant and complete for the model's purpose, without exclusions that could bias the projections.

sections.heading: Purpose and intended uses
sections.text: The Macroeconomic Scenario and Satellite Models (MDL-10) generate internally consistent macroeconomic scenarios and translate them into projected PD and LGD paths for the Bank's credit portfolios. The intended uses are: (a) forward-looking information for IFRS 9, namely the baseline, upside and downside scenarios, their probability weights and the scenario-conditional PD multipliers applied to the IFRS 9 PD models; (b) the ICAAP normative and economic perspectives; (c) the annual Group stress test and the reverse stress test; and (d) the calibration of the credit risk appetite early-warning levels. The model is a quantitative method whose output is used for financial reporting, risk measurement and capital planning, and is therefore managed across its full lifecycle under the Model Risk Management Policy. It is developed internally by the Scenario and Satellite Modelling team of Enterprise Stress Testing; the Bank does not use vendor scenarios, and the DNB projections used to anchor the baseline are an external input rather than a model component. This document describes model version 5.0, which results from the 2027 re-estimation on data up to 2026Q2 and the introduction of a commercial real estate price driver in the corporate PD satellite.

sections.heading: Model architecture
sections.text: The model consists of four components: (1) the scenario generation model, a Bayesian vector autoregression (BVAR) for six core Dutch variables with euro area GDP and the oil price as exogenous variables; (2) auxiliary equations for commercial real estate prices, credit spreads, equity prices, the exchange rate and the yield curve; (3) PD satellite models per portfolio, estimated as dynamic fixed-effects panel regressions of segment default rates; and (4) the LGD satellite for retail SME and corporates and the HPI linkage of the mortgage LGD models. The outputs are quarterly scenario paths over a projection horizon of three years, quarterly PD multipliers per segment and scenario, and LGD adjustments, delivered to the IFRS 9 calculation engine, the ICAAP projection tool and the stress test platform. The same satellite models are used for IFRS 9, stress testing and the ICAAP; the differences required by the purpose are limited to the scenarios applied and to the parameters to which the multipliers are applied (IFRS 9 point-in-time PDs, stress test point-in-time PDs and, for RWA, IRB rating migration). The model therefore translates stressed risk factors into internal PD and LGD parameters based on the Bank's historical experience, supplemented by the DNB projections and the CBS bankruptcy statistics as external benchmarks.

sections.heading: Scenario generation model
sections.text: The BVAR has two lags and six endogenous variables: quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth, the unemployment rate, quarter-on-quarter house price growth, the 3-month Euribor, the 10-year Dutch government bond yield and year-on-year HICP inflation. The joint estimation of these variables ensures that scenario paths are internally consistent: a GDP shock propagates to unemployment, house prices and interest rates through the estimated dynamics rather than through separately assumed paths. The model is estimated on 122 quarters (1996Q1–2026Q2) with dummy variables for 2020Q2–2020Q4 to prevent the COVID-19 quarters from dominating the estimated persistence. Stochastic simulation draws 10,000 paths from the posterior distribution of the parameters and the residual covariance matrix, which provides the predictive distribution used for the upside and downside scenarios, the weights and the severity calibration of the adverse scenario. The methodology is tailored to the Bank's risk profile, which is dominated by Dutch residential real estate, and the Bank fully understands and maintains the model code.

sections.heading: Satellite model structure and segmentation
sections.text: The PD satellite models are estimated per portfolio as logit(DR_s,t) = α_s + ρ·logit(DR_s,t−1) + β'X_t−l + ε_s,t, where DR_s,t is the four-quarter default rate of segment s, α_s a segment fixed effect and X the macroeconomic drivers with lag l. Segments are 8 mortgage segments (four indexed LTV bands with and without the Dutch national mortgage guarantee NHG), 4 consumer product segments, 6 retail SME sectors and 11 corporate sectors; common slope coefficients per portfolio are estimated because segment-specific slopes are not stable on 94 quarters. Standard errors are Driscoll–Kraay errors robust to heteroskedasticity, serial correlation and cross-sectional dependence, with a bandwidth of four quarters. The satellites project default rates at segment level; the PD multiplier for a segment and quarter is the ratio of the projected to the current default rate on the odds scale, which is applied to the facility-level PDs of the downstream models so that differences between facilities are preserved. The segments group exposures on shared credit risk characteristics (product, collateral, LTV band, sector), which are granular enough to capture differences in macroeconomic sensitivity. Key terms (default, default rate, loss given default, scenario, PD multiplier) are defined in Annex 1 and are identical for IFRS 9, stress testing and the ICAAP.

sections.heading: Alternatives for scenario generation
sections.text: Three alternatives were assessed for scenario generation against documented criteria (internal consistency, forecast performance, ability to generate a predictive distribution, transparency and maintainability): a frequentist VAR(2) (the approach of model version 3), a Bayesian VAR(2) with Minnesota prior, and a semi-structural model of the DNB type. The frequentist VAR was over-parameterised for six variables and 122 quarters (79 parameters) and produced unstable impulse responses; the semi-structural model was rejected because it requires calibration of many behavioural parameters by expert judgement and its maintenance exceeds the team's capacity. The BVAR reduced the root mean squared error of the four-quarter-ahead GDP forecast by 14% and of the unemployment forecast by 19% against the frequentist VAR in recursive forecasts from 2010, and was selected.

sections.heading: Alternatives for the satellite models
sections.text: Three alternatives were assessed for the PD satellites: (a) dynamic fixed-effects panel regression of logit default rates (selected); (b) a single-factor Vasicek credit cycle index model, in which a systematic factor Z_t is extracted from default rates and regressed on macroeconomic variables; (c) portfolio-level time-series regressions. The panel approach uses the cross-sectional variation of 29 segments, which reduces parameter uncertainty compared with portfolio-level regressions, and allows the CRE driver to be applied only to real estate and construction segments. The Vasicek model (b) has similar performance (out-of-time RMSE 6% higher) but imposes an asset-correlation assumption; it is retained as the challenger model required for Tier 1 satellite models. Links between risk factors and losses therefore rest on statistical models where data permit, and the results of the alternative approach are compared in section 7.6.

sections.heading: BVAR estimation
sections.text: The BVAR uses a Normal–inverse-Wishart prior with Minnesota moments: overall tightness 0.2, cross-variable shrinkage 0.5 and lag decay 1.0, selected by maximising the marginal likelihood over a grid, and a prior mean of a random walk for levels and white noise for growth rates. Posterior draws are generated directly from the conjugate posterior; 10,000 draws are used with the random seed 5021. All estimated impulse responses have the expected signs: a one-standard-deviation negative GDP shock raises unemployment by 0.19 percentage points after four quarters, lowers house price growth by 1.1 percentage points and lowers the 3-month Euribor by 12 basis points. The eigenvalues of the companion matrix at the posterior mean are below 0.97 in modulus, so the model is stable and projections revert to the unconditional mean.

sections.heading: Construction of the IFRS 9 scenarios
sections.text: The baseline is a conditional forecast of the BVAR in which GDP growth, unemployment and inflation for the first three years follow the latest DNB macroeconomic projections, and the other variables are projected conditionally on these paths. The upside and downside scenarios are the means of the simulated paths whose three-year cumulative GDP growth lies between the 85th and 95th percentile and between the 5th and 15th percentile of the predictive distribution respectively, re-centred on the conditional baseline. ECL is computed under at least the baseline, upside and downside scenarios, each with a written narrative, and is updated quarterly with the latest DNB projections or, between projection rounds, with the latest data. The explicit forecasts cover a reasonable and supportable forecast period of three years, after which the PD multipliers revert linearly to 1 (the long-run average) over eight quarters; this process determines how ECL is estimated for exposures whose life exceeds the forecast period. The current and forecast direction of economic conditions at the reporting date is thus reflected through the starting point of the conditional forecast and the scenario paths.

sections.heading: Scenario probability weights
sections.text: Scenario probability weights are determined quarterly from the BVAR predictive distribution: each of the 10,000 simulated paths is assigned to the nearest scenario by three-year cumulative GDP growth, and the share of paths assigned to each scenario is its quantitative weight. For the first quarter of 2027 this gives 21.6% for the upside, 52.9% for the baseline and 25.5% for the downside scenario. The Scenario Working Group proposes the final weights, which may deviate from the quantitative weights by expert judgement where risks are not reflected in the historical distribution; the weights for Q1 2027 were set at 20%, 50% and 30% to reflect trade policy and geopolitical risks (EJ-10-04). No scenario carries a weight below 10%, and the weights are approved quarterly by the Group Impairment Committee together with the scenarios and the ECL sensitivity to a 100% weighting of each scenario. The weighting results in an unbiased, probability-weighted ECL that reflects a range of possible outcomes rather than a single most likely scenario.

sections.heading: Adverse and reverse stress scenarios
sections.text: The ICAAP adverse scenario is designed by the Scenario Working Group from the material risks and vulnerabilities identified in the annual risk identification process, notably the concentration in Dutch residential real estate, commercial real estate, interest rate risk in the banking book and funding. Its narrative is written first and approved by the Stress Testing Steering Committee, after which the BVAR produces the paths conditional on the narrative's key shocks (GDP, house prices and the term premium), so that the quantified variables are consistent with the narrative. Severity is calibrated against historical episodes and the predictive distribution: the percentile or historical analogue of each key variable is documented in the scenario note, for example the three-year cumulative GDP growth at the 1.5th percentile of the BVAR distribution. The adverse scenario includes hypothetical, non-historical elements such as a trade-war-induced collapse of euro area exports combined with a term premium shock, and the scenario set spans mild (downside) to severe (adverse) degrees of severity. For the reverse stress test, the model is run backwards by searching over the scale of the adverse shocks until the CET1 ratio reaches the total SREP capital requirement, and the plausibility of the resulting scenario is assessed against the BVAR distribution.

sections.heading: Satellite variable selection and macro linkages
sections.text: Candidate drivers were selected on economic rationale, availability in the scenario set at the point of use and stability over time: unemployment, GDP growth, house price growth, CRE price growth, the 3-month Euribor, the 10-year yield, credit spreads, inflation and household disposable income, each at lags of zero to four quarters. The selection used univariate analysis (sign and significance of each driver and lag), followed by a multivariate specification search; correlated drivers (GDP growth and disposable income, correlation 0.81) were not combined in one equation, and every retained driver has the expected sign and a magnitude consistent with economic intuition. Each satellite documents its macro linkage: unemployment raises mortgage and consumer defaults through income loss (expected sign positive), house prices reduce mortgage defaults through the equity cushion and the possibility of sale (negative), GDP growth reduces business defaults through revenue (negative), interest rates raise SME defaults through debt service (positive), and CRE prices reduce real estate defaults through refinancing capacity (negative); lags reflect the time from shock to 90 days past due. Rejected alternatives are documented: house price growth in the consumer satellite (positive sign), inflation in the mortgage satellite (t = 0.9) and the 10-year yield in the corporate satellite (counter-intuitive sign), even though the latter improved the in-sample fit.

sections.heading: Translation into PD term structures
sections.text: For IFRS 9, the PD multipliers are applied to the point-in-time PD term structures of the IFRS 9 PD models for the three-year forecast period, after which they revert linearly to 1 over eight quarters, so that cumulative PD curves remain monotonically non-decreasing and marginal PDs non-negative. For the stress test and the ICAAP, the multipliers are applied to point-in-time PDs consistent with the scenario severity, and not to the through-the-cycle PDs or downturn LGDs used for own funds requirements. For the ICAAP RWA projection, stressed PDs are mapped to IRB rating grades so that rating migration increases RWA, and interest rate paths feed the prepayment and deposit models of ALM; these second-round effects are captured in the projection tool. sections.heading: Calibration to current conditions
sections.text: The satellite projections are anchored to current conditions: the starting default rate of each segment is the most recent observed four-quarter default rate, so that the projected PDs are point-in-time and reflect recently observed default rates rather than long-run averages. Historical relationships are applied to current and forecast macroeconomic conditions through the scenario paths, which adjusts the historical loss experience for conditions that did not affect the historical period. Beyond the forecast period, the reversion target is the long-run average default rate of each segment over 2003–2026, which is used only for the reversion and not as the point-in-time calibration target. No prudential conservatism is included in the IFRS 9 projections: the multipliers are unbiased estimates and no margin of conservatism, downturn component or floor is applied.

sections.text: Performance is assessed for the BVAR by recursive pseudo out-of-sample forecast errors, and for the satellite models by in-sample fit, leave-one-segment-out cross-validation, out-of-time projection errors on 2023Q1–2026Q2 and back-tests of projections under realised macroeconomic paths, with thresholds consistent with MV-HB-003. Discriminatory power metrics (AUC, Gini) are not used, because the satellite models project segment default rates over time and do not rank-order obligors. Performance is reported for each portfolio and each segment.

sections.heading: Out-of-sample and out-of-time results
sections.text: In the leave-one-segment-out cross-validation, the RMSE of the logit default rate increases by between 4% and 11% relative to in-sample, indicating that the common slopes are not driven by single segments. On the out-of-time sample 2023Q1–2026Q2, projected with the realised macroeconomic paths from the 2022Q4 starting point, the relative errors of the average four-quarter default rate are: mortgages 6.9%, consumer lending 11.4%, retail SME 17.8% and corporates 9.2%. The amber retail SME result is caused by the interest rate increase of 2022–2023, whose effect on SME defaults materialised faster than the estimated lag of two quarters; it is recorded as limitation LIM-10-08 and monitored. For the BVAR, the recursive four-quarter-ahead forecast RMSE since 2010 is 1.7 percentage points for GDP growth, 0.5 percentage points for unemployment and 4.1 percentage points for house price growth, 14% to 23% below a random-walk benchmark.

sections.heading: Back-test under realised macroeconomic paths
sections.text: Projections were back-tested by running the satellite models over three historical windows with the realised macroeconomic paths as scenarios: 2008Q1–2010Q4, 2011Q1–2013Q4 and 2020Q1–2022Q4. The projected cumulative three-year default rates deviate from the realised rates by −8% (mortgages), +5% (consumer lending), −12% (retail SME) and +7% (corporates) in the 2011–2013 window, which contains the Dutch housing downturn, and by less than 15% in all portfolios in the other windows. The satellite models thus reproduce the direction and magnitude of historical default rate movements in response to unemployment, house prices and GDP. The back-test validates the assumptions and parameters of the credit risk stress testing models quantitatively, as part of the annual assessment of the stress testing programme.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and inputs: the BVAR prior tightness (0.1 and 0.3 instead of 0.2), the satellite lag structure (one quarter shorter and longer), the exclusion of the moratoria quarters, the approximation-period dummy, the CRE interpolation method and the expert judgements EJ-10-03 to EJ-10-06. The largest sensitivities of the ICAAP adverse credit losses are to the lag structure (±EUR 96 million), the house price kink EJ-10-03 (EUR 61 million) and the prior tightness (±EUR 44 million); the IFRS 9 loss allowance changes by at most EUR 14 million in any sensitivity. The results show that the model's conclusions are robust to reasonable alternative assumptions, and the sensitivities are reported with the stress test results so that the uncertainty of the results is transparent.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions are: (a) the joint dynamics of the Dutch economy over 1996–2026 are informative for the next three years; (b) the relationship between macroeconomic drivers and segment default rates is stable and linear on the logit scale within the historical range; (c) the common slope within each portfolio applies to all its segments; (d) default rates revert to their long-run average after the forecast period; (e) the Bank's lending does not affect the macroeconomy. Assumption (a) is supported by the recursive forecast evaluation, (b) by the coefficient stability test (Chow test at 2016Q1, p = 0.34) and the extrapolation treatment, (c) by the leave-one-segment-out results, (d) by the stationarity of segment default rates (panel unit root test rejected at 1%) and (e) by the Bank's market share. The assumptions and their plausibility are communicated to the Stress Testing Steering Committee and the Group Impairment Committee with each scenario approval.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan
sections.text: The monitoring plan MP-10 v5.0 is part of this chapter; it was approved by the model owner on 14 May 2027 and reviewed by Model Validation on 7 May 2027. Monitoring is quarterly, as required for Tier 1 models, and results are reported within 45 days of the quarter end. The PSI of the segment composition against the development panel is reported as a stability indicator with the thresholds 0.10 and 0.25. The plan is updated with every model change and reviewed at least annually.

sections.heading: Purpose and intended uses
sections.text: The Macroeconomic Scenario and Satellite Models (MDL-10) generate internally consistent macroeconomic scenarios and translate them into projected PD and LGD paths for the Bank's credit portfolios. The intended uses are: (a) forward-looking information for IFRS 9, namely the baseline, upside and downside scenarios, their probability weights and the scenario-conditional PD multipliers applied to the IFRS 9 PD models; (b) the ICAAP normative and economic perspectives; (c) the annual Group stress test and the reverse stress test; and (d) the calibration of the credit risk appetite early-warning levels. The model is a quantitative method whose output is used for financial reporting, risk measurement and capital planning, and is therefore managed across its full lifecycle under the Model Risk Management Policy. It is developed internally by the Scenario and Satellite Modelling team of Enterprise Stress Testing; the Bank does not use vendor scenarios, and the DNB projections used to anchor the baseline are an external input rather than a model component. This document describes model version 5.0, which results from the 2027 re-estimation on data up to 2026Q2 and the introduction of a commercial real estate price driver in the corporate PD satellite.

sections.heading: Model architecture
sections.text: The model consists of four components: (1) the scenario generation model, a Bayesian vector autoregression (BVAR) for six core Dutch variables with euro area GDP and the oil price as exogenous variables; (2) auxiliary equations for commercial real estate prices, credit spreads, equity prices, the exchange rate and the yield curve; (3) PD satellite models per portfolio, estimated as dynamic fixed-effects panel regressions of segment default rates; and (4) the LGD satellite for retail SME and corporates and the HPI linkage of the mortgage LGD models. The outputs are quarterly scenario paths over a projection horizon of three years, quarterly PD multipliers per segment and scenario, and LGD adjustments, delivered to the IFRS 9 calculation engine, the ICAAP projection tool and the stress test platform. The same satellite models are used for IFRS 9, stress testing and the ICAAP; the differences required by the purpose are limited to the scenarios applied and to the parameters to which the multipliers are applied (IFRS 9 point-in-time PDs, stress test point-in-time PDs and, for RWA, IRB rating migration). The model therefore translates stressed risk factors into internal PD and LGD parameters based on the Bank's historical experience, supplemented by the DNB projections and the CBS bankruptcy statistics as external benchmarks.

sections.heading: Scenario generation model
sections.text: The BVAR has two lags and six endogenous variables: quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth, the unemployment rate, quarter-on-quarter house price growth, the 3-month Euribor, the 10-year Dutch government bond yield and year-on-year HICP inflation. The joint estimation of these variables ensures that scenario paths are internally consistent: a GDP shock propagates to unemployment, house prices and interest rates through the estimated dynamics rather than through separately assumed paths. The model is estimated on 122 quarters (1996Q1–2026Q2) with dummy variables for 2020Q2–2020Q4 to prevent the COVID-19 quarters from dominating the estimated persistence. sections.heading: Satellite model structure and segmentation
sections.text: The PD satellite models are estimated per portfolio as logit(DR_s,t) = α_s + ρ·logit(DR_s,t−1) + β'X_t−l + ε_s,t, where DR_s,t is the four-quarter default rate of segment s, α_s a segment fixed effect and X the macroeconomic drivers with lag l. Segments are 8 mortgage segments (four indexed LTV bands with and without the Dutch national mortgage guarantee NHG), 4 consumer product segments, 6 retail SME sectors and 11 corporate sectors; common slope coefficients per portfolio are estimated because segment-specific slopes are not stable on 94 quarters. Standard errors are Driscoll–Kraay errors robust to heteroskedasticity, serial correlation and cross-sectional dependence, with a bandwidth of four quarters. The satellites project default rates at segment level; the PD multiplier for a segment and quarter is the ratio of the projected to the current default rate on the odds scale, which is applied to the facility-level PDs of the downstream models so that differences between facilities are preserved. The segments group exposures on shared credit risk characteristics (product, collateral, LTV band, sector), which are granular enough to capture differences in macroeconomic sensitivity. Key terms (default, default rate, loss given default, scenario, PD multiplier) are defined in Annex 1 and are identical for IFRS 9, stress testing and the ICAAP.

sections.heading: Alternatives for scenario generation
sections.text: Three alternatives were assessed for scenario generation against documented criteria (internal consistency, forecast performance, ability to generate a predictive distribution, transparency and maintainability): a frequentist VAR(2) (the approach of model version 3), a Bayesian VAR(2) with Minnesota prior, and a semi-structural model of the DNB type. The frequentist VAR was over-parameterised for six variables and 122 quarters (79 parameters) and produced unstable impulse responses; the semi-structural model was rejected because it requires calibration of many behavioural parameters by expert judgement and its maintenance exceeds the team's capacity. The BVAR reduced the root mean squared error of the four-quarter-ahead GDP forecast by 14% and of the unemployment forecast by 19% against the frequentist VAR in recursive forecasts from 2010, and was selected.

sections.heading: Alternatives for the satellite models
sections.text: Three alternatives were assessed for the PD satellites: (a) dynamic fixed-effects panel regression of logit default rates (selected); (b) a single-factor Vasicek credit cycle index model, in which a systematic factor Z_t is extracted from default rates and regressed on macroeconomic variables; (c) portfolio-level time-series regressions. The panel approach uses the cross-sectional variation of 29 segments, which reduces parameter uncertainty compared with portfolio-level regressions, and allows the CRE driver to be applied only to real estate and construction segments. The Vasicek model (b) has similar performance (out-of-time RMSE 6% higher) but imposes an asset-correlation assumption; it is retained as the challenger model required for Tier 1 satellite models. Links between risk factors and losses therefore rest on statistical models where data permit, and the results of the alternative approach are compared in section 7.6.

sections.heading: BVAR estimation
sections.text: The BVAR uses a Normal–inverse-Wishart prior with Minnesota moments: overall tightness 0.2, cross-variable shrinkage 0.5 and lag decay 1.0, selected by maximising the marginal likelihood over a grid, and a prior mean of a random walk for levels and white noise for growth rates. Posterior draws are generated directly from the conjugate posterior; 10,000 draws are used with the random seed 5021. All estimated impulse responses have the expected signs: a one-standard-deviation negative GDP shock raises unemployment by 0.19 percentage points after four quarters, lowers house price growth by 1.1 percentage points and lowers the 3-month Euribor by 12 basis points. The eigenvalues of the companion matrix at the posterior mean are below 0.97 in modulus, so the model is stable and projections revert to the unconditional mean.

sections.heading: Construction of the IFRS 9 scenarios
sections.text: The baseline is a conditional forecast of the BVAR in which GDP growth, unemployment and inflation for the first three years follow the latest DNB macroeconomic projections, and the other variables are projected conditionally on these paths. The upside and downside scenarios are the means of the simulated paths whose three-year cumulative GDP growth lies between the 85th and 95th percentile and between the 5th and 15th percentile of the predictive distribution respectively, re-centred on the conditional baseline. ECL is computed under at least the baseline, upside and downside scenarios, each with a written narrative, and is updated quarterly with the latest DNB projections or, between projection rounds, with the latest data. The explicit forecasts cover a reasonable and supportable forecast period of three years, after which the PD multipliers revert linearly to 1 (the long-run average) over eight quarters; this process determines how ECL is estimated for exposures whose life exceeds the forecast period. The current and forecast direction of economic conditions at the reporting date is thus reflected through the starting point of the conditional forecast and the scenario paths.

sections.heading: Scenario probability weights
sections.text: Scenario probability weights are determined quarterly from the BVAR predictive distribution: each of the 10,000 simulated paths is assigned to the nearest scenario by three-year cumulative GDP growth, and the share of paths assigned to each scenario is its quantitative weight. For the first quarter of 2027 this gives 21.6% for the upside, 52.9% for the baseline and 25.5% for the downside scenario. The Scenario Working Group proposes the final weights, which may deviate from the quantitative weights by expert judgement where risks are not reflected in the historical distribution; the weights for Q1 2027 were set at 20%, 50% and 30% to reflect trade policy and geopolitical risks (EJ-10-04). No scenario carries a weight below 10%, and the weights are approved quarterly by the Group Impairment Committee together with the scenarios and the ECL sensitivity to a 100% weighting of each scenario. The weighting results in an unbiased, probability-weighted ECL that reflects a range of possible outcomes rather than a single most likely scenario.

sections.heading: Adverse and reverse stress scenarios
sections.text: The ICAAP adverse scenario is designed by the Scenario Working Group from the material risks and vulnerabilities identified in the annual risk identification process, notably the concentration in Dutch residential real estate, commercial real estate, interest rate risk in the banking book and funding. Its narrative is written first and approved by the Stress Testing Steering Committee, after which the BVAR produces the paths conditional on the narrative's key shocks (GDP, house prices and the term premium), so that the quantified variables are consistent with the narrative. Severity is calibrated against historical episodes and the predictive distribution: the percentile or historical analogue of each key variable is documented in the scenario note, for example the three-year cumulative GDP growth at the 1.5th percentile of the BVAR distribution. The adverse scenario includes hypothetical, non-historical elements such as a trade-war-induced collapse of euro area exports combined with a term premium shock, and the scenario set spans mild (downside) to severe (adverse) degrees of severity. For the reverse stress test, the model is run backwards by searching over the scale of the adverse shocks until the CET1 ratio reaches the total SREP capital requirement, and the plausibility of the resulting scenario is assessed against the BVAR distribution.

sections.heading: Satellite variable selection and macro linkages
sections.text: Candidate drivers were selected on economic rationale, availability in the scenario set at the point of use and stability over time: unemployment, GDP growth, house price growth, CRE price growth, the 3-month Euribor, the 10-year yield, credit spreads, inflation and household disposable income, each at lags of zero to four quarters. The selection used univariate analysis (sign and significance of each driver and lag), followed by a multivariate specification search; correlated drivers (GDP growth and disposable income, correlation 0.81) were not combined in one equation, and every retained driver has the expected sign and a magnitude consistent with economic intuition. Each satellite documents its macro linkage: unemployment raises mortgage and consumer defaults through income loss (expected sign positive), house prices reduce mortgage defaults through the equity cushion and the possibility of sale (negative), GDP growth reduces business defaults through revenue (negative), interest rates raise SME defaults through debt service (positive), and CRE prices reduce real estate defaults through refinancing capacity (negative); lags reflect the time from shock to 90 days past due. Rejected alternatives are documented: house price growth in the consumer satellite (positive sign), inflation in the mortgage satellite (t = 0.9) and the 10-year yield in the corporate satellite (counter-intuitive sign), even though the latter improved the in-sample fit.

sections.heading: Translation into PD term structures
sections.text: For IFRS 9, the PD multipliers are applied to the point-in-time PD term structures of the IFRS 9 PD models for the three-year forecast period, after which they revert linearly to 1 over eight quarters, so that cumulative PD curves remain monotonically non-decreasing and marginal PDs non-negative. For the stress test and the ICAAP, the multipliers are applied to point-in-time PDs consistent with the scenario severity, and not to the through-the-cycle PDs or downturn LGDs used for own funds requirements. For the ICAAP RWA projection, stressed PDs are mapped to IRB rating grades so that rating migration increases RWA, and interest rate paths feed the prepayment and deposit models of ALM; these second-round effects are captured in the projection tool. Feedback effects of the Bank's own deleveraging on the macroeconomy are not modelled, because the Bank's share of Dutch lending is too small to affect aggregate outcomes; this omission is justified in the limitations log.

sections.heading: Calibration to current conditions
sections.text: The satellite projections are anchored to current conditions: the starting default rate of each segment is the most recent observed four-quarter default rate, so that the projected PDs are point-in-time and reflect recently observed default rates rather than long-run averages. Historical relationships are applied to current and forecast macroeconomic conditions through the scenario paths, which adjusts the historical loss experience for conditions that did not affect the historical period. Beyond the forecast period, the reversion target is the long-run average default rate of each segment over 2003–2026, which is used only for the reversion and not as the point-in-time calibration target. No prudential conservatism is included in the IFRS 9 projections: the multipliers are unbiased estimates and no margin of conservatism, downturn component or floor is applied.

sections.heading: Performance framework
sections.text: Performance is assessed for the BVAR by recursive pseudo out-of-sample forecast errors, and for the satellite models by in-sample fit, leave-one-segment-out cross-validation, out-of-time projection errors on 2023Q1–2026Q2 and back-tests of projections under realised macroeconomic paths, with thresholds consistent with MV-HB-003. Acceptance thresholds, approved by MRM for this model under MRM-STD-040 §5.6, are: out-of-time relative error of the four-quarter default rate per portfolio green below 15%, amber 15% to 30%, red above 30%; two-sided Jeffreys test of projected against realised default rates per portfolio amber below p = 5% and red below p = 1%. sections.heading: Back-test under realised macroeconomic paths
sections.text: Projections were back-tested by running the satellite models over three historical windows with the realised macroeconomic paths as scenarios: 2008Q1–2010Q4, 2011Q1–2013Q4 and 2020Q1–2022Q4. The projected cumulative three-year default rates deviate from the realised rates by −8% (mortgages), +5% (consumer lending), −12% (retail SME) and +7% (corporates) in the 2011–2013 window, which contains the Dutch housing downturn, and by less than 15% in all portfolios in the other windows. The satellite models thus reproduce the direction and magnitude of historical default rate movements in response to unemployment, house prices and GDP. The back-test validates the assumptions and parameters of the credit risk stress testing models quantitatively, as part of the annual assessment of the stress testing programme.

sections.heading: Extrapolation and plausibility
sections.text: Satellite models were tested under scenario values outside the historical range of the development data: house price declines of up to 30% year on year, unemployment up to 12% and GDP contractions of up to 8% year on year. Because the logit specification is linear in the drivers, the mortgage PD response to house price declines beyond the historical minimum (−9.4% year on year in 2013Q2) would understate the non-linear effect of negative equity; therefore, for house price growth below −10% year on year, the house price coefficient is multiplied by 1.5 for the part of the decline beyond −10% (EJ-10-03). With this treatment, the mortgage PD multiplier under a 30% house price decline combined with 12% unemployment is 4.6, compared with 3.7 without it and 5.1 in the challenger model, which is considered plausible against the 2011–2013 experience. Plausibility of the adverse scenario results was reviewed by the Stress Testing Steering Committee on 23 February 2027.

sections.text: A challenger model is maintained for each satellite, the Vasicek credit cycle index model of section 4.2, as required for Tier 1 satellite models. As an external benchmark, the default rate increases in the adverse scenario were compared with the realised Dutch default rates of 2009–2013 and with the credit loss rates in the EBA EU-wide stress test adverse scenarios for Dutch banks, which lie within the range of the model results.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and inputs: the BVAR prior tightness (0.1 and 0.3 instead of 0.2), the satellite lag structure (one quarter shorter and longer), the exclusion of the moratoria quarters, the approximation-period dummy, the CRE interpolation method and the expert judgements EJ-10-03 to EJ-10-06. The largest sensitivities of the ICAAP adverse credit losses are to the lag structure (±EUR 96 million), the house price kink EJ-10-03 (EUR 61 million) and the prior tightness (±EUR 44 million); the IFRS 9 loss allowance changes by at most EUR 14 million in any sensitivity. The results show that the model's conclusions are robust to reasonable alternative assumptions, and the sensitivities are reported with the stress test results so that the uncertainty of the results is transparent.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions are: (a) the joint dynamics of the Dutch economy over 1996–2026 are informative for the next three years; (b) the relationship between macroeconomic drivers and segment default rates is stable and linear on the logit scale within the historical range; (c) the common slope within each portfolio applies to all its segments; (d) default rates revert to their long-run average after the forecast period; (e) the Bank's lending does not affect the macroeconomy. Assumption (a) is supported by the recursive forecast evaluation, (b) by the coefficient stability test (Chow test at 2016Q1, p = 0.34) and the extrapolation treatment, (c) by the leave-one-segment-out results, (d) by the stationarity of segment default rates (panel unit root test rejected at 1%) and (e) by the Bank's market share. The assumptions and their plausibility are communicated to the Stress Testing Steering Committee and the Group Impairment Committee with each scenario approval.

sections.text: The expert judgement log of MDL-10 (DOC-MDL10-EJLOG) records every expert judgement with type, lifecycle stage, affected variable or segment, rationale, evidence, alternatives, quantified impact, proposer, approver, approval date, review date and expiry conditions, and is referenced in this MDD and, for EJ-10-01, in the RDS documentation. EJ-10-01 Chow–Lin interpolation of the CRE index (data treatment; low); EJ-10-02 COVID-19 dummies in the BVAR (design; medium; adverse credit losses +EUR 38 million against no dummies); EJ-10-03 house price kink below −10% (extrapolation; high; +EUR 61 million; addresses limitation LIM-10-01 until a non-linear satellite is developed for version 6.0 in 2028); EJ-10-04 downside tilt of the scenario weights (weights; medium; IFRS 9 loss allowance +EUR 6 million); EJ-10-05 LGD floor in the adverse scenario (calibration; medium; +EUR 27 million); EJ-10-06 additional drawdown of undrawn limits (EAD; medium; +EUR 19 million). sections.heading: Purpose, scope and approvals
sections.text: This note documents the macroeconomic scenarios produced with model version 4.1 of MDL-10 for the IFRS 9 reporting date 31 March 2027 and for the ICAAP 2027 stress test, together with the scenario probability weights and their rationale. The IFRS 9 scenarios, the probability weights and the ECL sensitivity to a 100% weighting of each scenario were approved by the Group Impairment Committee on 24 March 2027. The scenarios form part of the stress testing programme 2027 approved by the Management Board on 26 January 2027.

sections.heading: Starting point
sections.text: In 2026 Dutch real GDP grew by 1.6%, unemployment rose from 3.7% to 4.1%, house prices increased by 6.8%, HICP inflation averaged 2.9%, and at year-end the 3-month Euribor stood at 2.0% and the 10-year Dutch government bond yield at 2.8%. The euro area economy grew by 1.1%, with downside risks from trade tariffs imposed during 2026 and from elevated public debt in several member states. The starting point reflects the current conditions at the reporting date, and the scenarios project the forecast direction of these conditions over the next three years. All data are taken from the MDP vintage of 12 March 2027, which includes the CBS flash estimate for 2026Q4.

sections.text: The baseline follows the DNB macroeconomic projections of December 2026: real GDP growth of 1.4%, 1.3% and 1.4% in 2027–2029, unemployment of 4.2%, 4.2% and 4.1%, house price growth of 4.5%, 3.0% and 2.5%, a 3-month Euribor of 2.0%, 2.1% and 2.2%, a 10-year yield of 2.9%, 3.0% and 3.1%, and inflation of 2.6%, 2.2% and 2.0%. The baseline is identical to the macroeconomic scenario of the financial plan 2027–2029 and the capital plan, and to the ICAAP baseline, so that forward-looking information is consistent across financial statements, budgets and capital planning. The house price path includes an expert adjustment of −1.0 percentage point in 2027 for the announced reduction of mortgage interest deductibility, approved by the model owner on 17 March 2027 (see section 9). The use of the DNB projections as anchor is consistent with generally accepted forecasting practice and supported by the BVAR, which projects all other variables conditionally on them.

sections.heading: Upside and downside scenarios
sections.text: The upside scenario (faster disinflation, easing of trade tensions and stronger investment) has GDP growth of 2.4%, 2.1% and 1.8%, unemployment of 3.8%, 3.7% and 3.7% and house price growth of 7.0%, 5.0% and 3.5%. The downside scenario (escalating trade tariffs, weaker euro area demand and a correction of the housing market) has GDP growth of −0.6%, 0.4% and 1.3%, unemployment of 4.9%, 5.6% and 5.4%, and house price growth of −3.9%, −2.6% and 1.2%. Both are derived from the 85th–95th and 5th–15th percentile ranges of the three-year cumulative GDP growth in the BVAR predictive distribution and each has a written narrative, so that the ECL reflects a range of possible outcomes rather than a single scenario. The downside scenario includes outcomes in which credit losses occur at levels well above the baseline, so that ECL reflects the possibility of loss even where the probability-weighted outlook is benign.

sections.heading: Scenario probability weights
sections.text: The quantitative weights from the BVAR predictive distribution are 21.6% (upside), 52.9% (baseline) and 25.5% (downside), obtained by assigning each of the 10,000 simulated paths to the nearest scenario by three-year cumulative GDP growth. The Scenario Working Group proposed, and the Group Impairment Committee approved, weights of 20%, 50% and 30%, adding 4.5 percentage points to the downside scenario because trade policy and geopolitical risks are judged to be larger than reflected in the 1996–2026 history (EJ-10-04). The size of the downside tilt is based on the judgement of the Working Group; its effect on the loss allowance is +EUR 6 million compared with the quantitative weights. No scenario weight is below 10%.

sections.heading: ICAAP adverse scenario narrative
sections.text: The adverse scenario "Trade shock and housing correction" addresses the Bank's material vulnerabilities from the 2026 risk identification: an escalation of tariffs triggers a global recession and a collapse of euro area exports, financial markets reprice risk with a term premium shock, and the Dutch housing and commercial real estate markets correct sharply as unemployment rises and mortgage rates increase. The quantified paths are: GDP growth of −2.9%, −1.6% and 0.8% in 2027–2029 (peak-to-trough −4.9%), unemployment rising to 8.1% in 2028Q4, house prices falling 22.5% peak to trough, CRE prices falling 31%, the 3-month Euribor falling to 0.6% as the ECB eases, the 10-year yield rising to 3.7% because of the term premium, the iBoxx spread widening by 250 basis points, equity prices falling 38% and the euro depreciating 12% against the dollar. The narrative is institution-specific: it combines market-wide stress with the concentration of the Bank in Dutch residential real estate and its funding reliance on retail deposits and covered bonds, and considers the interaction between solvency and funding stress through higher funding spreads. The scenario is severe but plausible and includes a severe economic downturn for the capital adequacy assessment and capital planning.

sections.heading: Severity calibration
sections.text: Severity is calibrated against the BVAR predictive distribution and historical episodes: the three-year cumulative GDP growth corresponds to the 1.5th percentile of the distribution, the unemployment peak to the 2nd percentile and the three-year cumulative house price change to the 1st percentile. As historical analogues, the GDP contraction is comparable in depth to the 2008–2009 recession, the house price decline exceeds the 2008–2013 correction of about 20% and occurs over two years instead of five, and the unemployment peak exceeds the 2014 peak. The CRE price decline of 31% is calibrated to the fall in Dutch office values between 2008 and 2014, adjusted for the higher vacancy of secondary offices. Severity was challenged by Model Validation and by the Stress Testing Steering Committee, which concluded that the scenario is more severe than the IFRS 9 downside scenario, as intended, and has a material impact on the CET1 ratio.

sections.heading: Description and rationale
sections.text: The change re-estimates the BVAR and the satellite models on data up to 2026Q2, shortens the Euribor lag in the retail SME satellite from three to two quarters, and adds the year-on-year CRE price growth as a driver for the corporate real estate and construction segments. The rationale is the amber projection error of the retail SME satellite in 2026, the instability of the SME Euribor coefficient, and the missing transmission of commercial real estate prices, which in version 4.1 was covered only through GDP. The change was recorded in the change log of the model inventory on 12 October 2026, before development and before implementation in production. The re-estimation and the new driver address related deficiencies and are therefore assessed as one change.

deficiencies.rationale: The quantitative weights (21.6/52.9/25.5) are derived from the BVAR predictive distribution. The approved weights (20/50/30), however, add 4.5 percentage points to the downside scenario on the Working Group's judgement, and no quantitative rationale is given for the size of this tilt.

mitigation.text: Quantify the downside tilt, for example with a tariff-shock scenario probability or a stressed predictive distribution. Document the derivation in the quarterly scenario note and in EJ-10-04.

deficiencies.rationale: Extrapolation tests beyond the historical range cover house prices, unemployment and GDP only. The new CRE driver of the corporate satellite is not tested, although the adverse CRE decline (−31%) lies outside the historical range of the development data.

mitigation.text: Extend the extrapolation tests of MDD section 7.4 to CRE price declines beyond the historical range. Document any required treatment.

deficiencies.rationale: The ICAAP 2026 baseline was compared with 2026 realised outcomes, but the −7% deviation for retail SME was neither analysed nor included in the report to the Stress Testing Steering Committee.

mitigation.text: Complete the deviation analysis for retail SME and report it to the Stress Testing Steering Committee before the ICAAP 2028 cycle.

deficiencies.rationale: The MDD states that the out-of-time sample 2023Q1–2026Q2 was not used for variable selection. Validation's review of the estimation repository shows that the lag-selection script select_lags.py ran on the full panel to 2026Q2. Repeating the selection on data to 2022Q4 selects house price growth at lag 2 instead of lag 1, and the out-of-time relative error for mortgages rises from 6.9% to 9.8%. The out-of-time test is therefore not independent.

mitigation.text: Repeat the variable and lag selection on the estimation sample only, re-perform the out-of-time tests, and document the sample used by every selection step.

deficiencies.rationale: The CRE coefficient of the corporate satellite (−0.012, t = −2.7) is reported as significant using Driscoll–Kraay standard errors. With two-way clustering by sector and quarter, which Validation considers appropriate for 11 sectors with a common CRE shock, t = −1.6, so the new driver is not significant at the 5% level.

mitigation.text: Justify the choice of standard errors or re-specify the CRE linkage, for example by pooling real estate and construction or using a longer CRE series. Retain the driver only if it is significant under robust inference.
